subtopic_detail: Constant pacing ten days into antipsychotic treatment in a young man whose psychotic symptoms are simultaneously improving
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar on an acute inpatient unit reviewing a 24 year old man admitted ten days ago with a first episode of psychosis. He was started on aripiprazole 10 mg daily and the dose was increased to 20 mg daily four days ago.

The nursing staff report that he has been walking the length of the corridor almost continuously since yesterday and will not stay seated for meals. When you ask him about it he says he feels like he has to jump out of his skin, that the feeling sits in his legs, and that walking is the only thing that eases it. He tells you the voices have become much quieter over the past week and he no longer believes his neighbours are recording him. He is oriented and cooperative, his tone is normal with no cogwheeling, his temperature is 36.9 degrees C and his creatine kinase is 118 U/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96 per minute, blood pressure 124/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Continuous pacing with an inability to remain seated, normal tone with no cogwheel rigidity, no tremor, no diaphoresis, oriented in time place and person
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 118 U/L (30-200), white cell count 7.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), urea electrolytes and creatinine within normal limits, urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Reduce the aripiprazole dose and start propranolol 10 mg three times daily
options.rationale: A subjective inner restlessness localised to the legs and relieved by movement, appearing days after a dose increase, is akathisia, and the primary treatment is to reduce the causative dose because the effect is dose related. Propranolol is the best supported adjunct in Australian practice while the dose change takes effect (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Add benztropine 1 mg twice daily to treat the extrapyramidal side effect
options.rationale: Anticholinergics work for acute dystonia and drug induced parkinsonism, both of which require rigidity, bradykinesia or sustained muscle spasm that this man does not have. Trials in akathisia specifically have shown no benefit over placebo, which is what separates it from the other extrapyramidal syndromes (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Increase the aripiprazole dose since the agitation reflects ongoing psychosis
options.rationale: Reading this as psychotic agitation and escalating the dose is the error that turns a treatable side effect into a crisis, and it is contradicted by his account of quieter voices and resolved persecutory beliefs. Untreated akathisia is a recognised contributor to suicidal acts during admission (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia).
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia

options.text: Add regular diazepam 5 mg twice daily and continue the current medication
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines do relieve akathisia and are a reasonable second line adjunct, but using one while holding the causative dose treats the symptom and leaves the cause running. Dose reduction is the intervention that resolves the problem rather than covering it (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Cease the aripiprazole and give intramuscular haloperidol for the agitation
options.rationale: A high potency typical antipsychotic carries a higher akathisia rate than the drug he is already taking, so this would intensify precisely the symptom being treated. Abrupt cessation also throws away a regimen that is working on his psychosis (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: Akathisia appears in roughly a fifth to a quarter of patients starting or escalating an antipsychotic and is most often mistaken for worsening psychotic agitation or for anxiety. The defining feature is subjective: an inner restlessness, usually referred to the legs, that is temporarily relieved by moving, which separates it from the objective slowness of parkinsonism and from the suppressible oro lingual movements of tardive dyskinesia. It matters because it is genuinely distressing and has been linked to treatment non adherence, aggression and suicide during admission. Management is dose reduction or a switch to a lower risk agent first, with propranolol as the best supported adjunct and a benzodiazepine as an alternative, while anticholinergics have consistently failed to show benefit. Objective rating with a structured akathisia scale at each dose change catches it earlier than waiting for the patient to volunteer it.
key_points: Akathisia is defined by subjective inner restlessness relieved by movement
It appears within days to weeks of starting or increasing an antipsychotic
Dose reduction or a switch is first line, with propranolol as the preferred adjunct
Anticholinergics are ineffective in akathisia despite working for other extrapyramidal effects
Normal tone, temperature and creatine kinase exclude neuroleptic malignant syndrome
explanation.pearls: Ask the patient directly whether the restlessness is inside them or only in how they look, because a patient who paces but denies any inner urge to move is far more likely to have psychomotor agitation, and only the inner urge responds to propranolol.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia

subtopic_detail: Timing of birth at 38 weeks for a woman on insulin whose estimated foetal weight sits just below the threshold that would prompt discussion of caesarean
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in the diabetes in pregnancy clinic reviewing a 32 year old woman at 38 weeks and one day in her second pregnancy. Gestational diabetes was diagnosed at 26 weeks and she has been on insulin since 30 weeks, currently 22 units of isophane at night with three pre meal rapid acting doses.

Her capillary glucose diary over the past fortnight shows fasting readings between 4.8 and 5.2 mmol/L and two hour postprandial readings between 6.1 and 6.8 mmol/L. Her first baby was born vaginally at 39 weeks weighing 3620 g with no difficulty at the shoulders and no perineal trauma beyond a second degree tear. A growth ultrasound performed yesterday gives an estimated foetal weight of 4350 g on the 98th centile with a normal amniotic fluid index and normal umbilical artery Dopplers. On abdominal examination the presentation is cephalic with the head three fifths palpable, and vaginal examination shows a cervix 2 cm long, soft, mid position and 1 cm dilated.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 84 per minute, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent, temperature 36.8 degrees C, foetal heart rate 145 per minute
data_table.Investigations: Fasting capillary glucose 4.8-5.2 mmol/L (target less than 5.1), two hour postprandial 6.1-6.8 mmol/L (target less than 6.7), haemoglobin 118 g/L (115-165)
data_table.Imaging: Estimated foetal weight 4350 g on the 98th centile, amniotic fluid index 14 cm, umbilical artery Dopplers within normal limits, cephalic presentation

lead_in: What would you first recommend regarding the timing and mode of her birth?

options.text: Recommend elective caesarean section this week because of the estimated weight
options.rationale: Discussion of planned caesarean for suspected macrosomia in diabetes is triggered at an estimated foetal weight of about 4500 g, and this estimate of 4350 g sits below it with a previous uncomplicated vaginal birth in her favour. Third trimester weight estimates also carry an error of around 10 to 15 per cent in either direction, which is why they anchor a conversation rather than a decision (Source: RANZCOG: Diagnosis and management of gestational diabetes).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Diagnosis and management of gestational diabetes

options.text: Await spontaneous labour and reassess her again at 40 weeks gestation
options.rationale: Insulin treated gestational diabetes carries a stillbirth risk that rises through the late term period, which is why birth is planned rather than awaited once 38 to 39 weeks is reached. Waiting also allows further foetal growth in the fortnight when it accelerates fastest (Source: RANZCOG: Diagnosis and management of gestational diabetes).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Diagnosis and management of gestational diabetes

options.text: Repeat the growth scan in two weeks and decide on the timing after that
options.rationale: A repeat scan would report at 40 weeks, past the window in which birth is recommended for insulin treated disease, and serial estimates in the same fortnight do not improve accuracy enough to change the plan. The decision here rests on the insulin requirement and gestation rather than on a refined weight estimate (Source: RANZCOG: Diagnosis and management of gestational diabetes).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Diagnosis and management of gestational diabetes

options.text: Recommend induction of labour this week after discussing the options with her
options.rationale: Insulin treated gestational diabetes is an indication for birth at 38 to 39 weeks, and with a favourable cervix, a cephalic presentation and a previous vaginal birth of a 3620 g baby, induction is the appropriate route at an estimated weight below the caesarean discussion threshold. Induction for suspected macrosomia also reduces shoulder dystocia without increasing caesarean rates in randomised data (Source: RANZCOG: Diagnosis and management of gestational diabetes).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Diagnosis and management of gestational diabetes

options.text: Stop her insulin now and plan an induction of labour at 41 weeks gestation
options.rationale: Insulin is continued antenatally while glucose targets require it and is stopped after birth rather than before it, since withdrawal now would allow the maternal hyperglycaemia that drives foetal insulin mediated growth to resume. Planning birth at 41 weeks compounds this by extending the exposure (Source: Australasian Diabetes in Pregnancy Society: Gestational diabetes management).
source_refs: Australasian Diabetes in Pregnancy Society: Gestational diabetes management

explanation.summary: Timing of birth in gestational diabetes is graded by whether pharmacological treatment is required, because insulin or metformin treated disease carries the higher stillbirth risk and is planned for birth at 38 to 39 weeks, while diet controlled disease with normal growth can usually reach 40 to 41 weeks. Suspected macrosomia is a separate axis, and the evidence for elective caesarean rests on an estimated foetal weight of about 4500 g in diabetes or 5000 g without it, thresholds that acknowledge how imprecise third trimester estimation is. The Australian approach to a large baby with a favourable cervix and a previous vaginal birth is induction rather than caesarean, and randomised evidence supports reduced shoulder dystocia with induction for suspected macrosomia. Intrapartum care includes hourly capillary glucose monitoring with a dextrose and insulin infusion if levels exceed target, and insulin is ceased immediately after birth. The neonate needs early feeding and blood glucose monitoring for neonatal hypoglycaemia.
key_points: Insulin treated gestational diabetes prompts planned birth at 38 to 39 weeks
Diet controlled disease with normal growth can usually continue to 40 to 41 weeks
Caesarean discussion for macrosomia in diabetes starts around an estimated weight of 4500 g
Third trimester weight estimates carry an error of roughly 10 to 15 per cent
Insulin is ceased after birth, not before, and the baby needs glucose monitoring
explanation.pearls: Check the maternal capillary glucose hourly in established labour and aim to keep it between 4 and 7 mmol/L, since intrapartum hyperglycaemia in the hours before birth is what drives reactive neonatal hypoglycaemia regardless of how well controlled the pregnancy was.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Diagnosis and management of gestational diabetes
Australasian Diabetes in Pregnancy Society: Gestational diabetes management

subtopic_detail: Eight months of inflammatory back pain in a young man whose sacroiliac radiographs and inflammatory markers are both normal
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar in a rapid access clinic seeing a 26 year old carpenter with eight months of lower back and buttock pain. He wakes at about four in the morning with the pain and has to get out of bed and move around, and he describes stiffness lasting well over an hour each morning that eases as the day goes on.

The pain alternates between the left and the right buttock from week to week and is worse on a rest day than on a work day. Ten months ago he had a painful red left eye that an optometrist referred urgently and that settled on steroid drops over three weeks. His father has psoriasis. On examination lumbar flexion is reduced with a Schober increase of 3.5 cm, and there is tenderness over both sacroiliac joints with no neurological deficit and negative straight leg raise. His C reactive protein is 4 mg/L and his erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 9 mm/h, and plain radiographs of the sacroiliac joints performed last month were reported as normal.

data_table.Examination: Modified Schober increase 3.5 cm, tenderness over both sacroiliac joints, full hip range of movement, normal lower limb power sensation and reflexes, negative straight leg raise bilaterally
data_table.Investigations: C reactive protein 4 mg/L (less than 5), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 9 mm/h (less than 15), full blood count within normal limits, rheumatoid factor and cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody negative
data_table.Imaging: Anteroposterior pelvis radiograph reported as showing normal sacroiliac joints

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Order HLA-B27 testing and make the diagnosis if the result comes back positive
options.rationale: HLA-B27 contributes to a probabilistic classification but cannot make the diagnosis on its own, since it is carried by about 8 per cent of the Australian population and is absent in roughly 10 to 20 per cent of affected patients. It supports rather than confirms, and it does not show whether inflammation is active now (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Axial spondyloarthritis).

options.text: Arrange MRI of the sacroiliac joints looking for active inflammatory change
options.rationale: Structural erosion takes years to become visible on plain films, so a normal radiograph in a young patient with eight months of symptoms indicates non radiographic disease rather than absence of disease, and MRI detects the bone marrow oedema that is present long before that. A normal C reactive protein is also expected here, since inflammatory markers are normal in around 40 to 50 per cent of cases and cannot be used to exclude the diagnosis (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Axial spondyloarthritis).

options.text: Arrange CT of the sacroiliac joints to detect early erosive bony change
options.rationale: CT resolves cortical erosion better than plain film but shows only structural damage, which is the late finding, and it delivers substantial pelvic radiation to a young man. It differs from the preferred imaging in exactly this way: it sees the scar rather than the fire (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Axial spondyloarthritis).

options.text: Refer him for a graded exercise programme and review him again in six months
options.rationale: Exercise therapy is a genuine part of long term management but deferring the diagnosis by another six months forfeits the window in which treatment limits structural progression. The average delay from symptom onset to diagnosis in this condition is already measured in years (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology).

options.text: Arrange lumbar spine MRI to look for a disc protrusion causing his symptoms
options.rationale: Discogenic pain is worse with activity and relieved by rest, whereas this man is worse on rest days and better with movement, and he has no radicular signs or positive straight leg raise. Imaging the lumbar spine also misses the sacroiliac joints, which are where the diagnostic finding lies (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology).

explanation.summary: Inflammatory back pain is defined by onset before the age of 45, insidious onset, morning stiffness beyond 30 minutes, improvement with exercise but not with rest, and night pain that wakes the patient in the second half of the night. Recognition of non radiographic axial spondyloarthritis changed practice by accepting that patients can have active sacroiliitis on MRI years before radiographic erosion appears, and that a normal radiograph therefore excludes nothing in a young patient. Extra articular features carry heavy diagnostic weight and include acute anterior uveitis, psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease, enthesitis and dactylitis, along with a family history of any of these. Normal inflammatory markers occur in roughly half of patients and are not a rule out. Treatment begins with regular non steroidal anti inflammatory drugs and structured exercise, escalating to tumour necrosis factor or interleukin 17 inhibitors when disease activity persists.
key_points: Night pain waking the patient with morning stiffness over an hour, better with movement, defines inflammatory back pain
Normal sacroiliac radiographs do not exclude the diagnosis in a patient under 45
MRI detects bone marrow oedema years before structural erosion is visible
Inflammatory markers are normal in about half of patients
Acute anterior uveitis and a family history of psoriasis are strong supporting features
explanation.pearls: Acute anterior uveitis occurs in about a third of patients with axial spondyloarthritis and often precedes the back pain, so a young adult presenting with a first unilateral painful red eye should be asked directly about early morning back stiffness lasting more than half an hour.

subtopic_detail: Deciding whether a six year old using reliever three to four times a week has crossed the threshold for regular preventer treatment
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a six year old boy whose mother has brought him for a routine asthma check. He was diagnosed eighteen months ago and uses salbutamol through a spacer as needed, with no regular preventer.

Over the past three months his mother has given salbutamol three or four times most weeks, usually before school when he is coughing, and he has woken coughing at night about twice a month. He has missed two days of school this term with chest symptoms and stops to catch his breath partway through a soccer game that he used to finish. He has not needed oral steroids or an emergency department visit in the past year. His growth is tracking along the 60th centile for height and weight, and you watch him use the spacer correctly with a good seal and adequate breaths. On examination his chest is clear with no wheeze at rest and his oxygen saturation is 98 per cent on room air.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88 per minute, blood pressure 100/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Chest clear with no wheeze or prolonged expiration at rest, no chest wall deformity, correct spacer technique demonstrated with good mask seal
data_table.Growth: Height and weight both on the 60th centile with no fall in centile over eighteen months

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Continue salbutamol as needed and check his inhaler technique again in three months
options.rationale: Reliever use on three or more days a week, night waking and exercise limitation together define poor symptom control, which is precisely the trigger for adding a preventer rather than for another period of observation. His technique has already been directly observed and is correct, so there is no remediable cause to review (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook).

options.text: Start a combination inhaled corticosteroid and long acting beta2 agonist inhaler
options.rationale: Combination therapy is the next step up if symptoms persist despite regular low dose inhaled corticosteroid, not the entry point, and long acting beta2 agonists are not recommended as initial preventer treatment in children of this age. Starting here also makes it impossible to know whether the corticosteroid alone would have sufficed (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook).

options.text: Start montelukast 5 mg each evening as his regular preventer medication instead
options.rationale: A leukotriene receptor antagonist is a second line preventer in children, less effective than inhaled corticosteroid, and carries a Therapeutic Goods Administration warning about neuropsychiatric effects including sleep disturbance and behavioural change. It is reserved for children who cannot use an inhaled corticosteroid (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook).

options.text: Start a two week course of oral prednisolone and review his symptoms afterwards
options.rationale: Oral corticosteroids treat acute exacerbations over three days, and a fortnight of systemic steroid for stable interval symptoms exposes him to adrenal suppression and growth effects without altering the underlying airway inflammation. Nothing in the current examination indicates an exacerbation (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook).

options.text: Start a regular low dose inhaled corticosteroid taken through his existing spacer
options.rationale: Symptoms or reliever use on more than two days per week, any night waking due to asthma, or activity limitation each independently indicate poorly controlled asthma and warrant a regular preventer, and he meets all three. Low dose inhaled corticosteroid is the first line preventer for a child of this age and is delivered through the spacer he is already using correctly (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook).

explanation.summary: Australian asthma control in children is assessed over the preceding four weeks against four questions covering daytime symptoms, reliever use, night waking and activity limitation, with more than two days a week of symptoms or reliever use marking the boundary of good control. A child with any of these features is not adequately managed on reliever alone, and low dose inhaled corticosteroid is the first line preventer for children aged six and over. Before escalating any preventer, adherence, inhaler technique, trigger exposure such as household smoking, and comorbid rhinitis should be reviewed, and a written asthma action plan updated. Growth is monitored because inhaled corticosteroids produce a small reduction in growth velocity in the first year of use, largely without affecting final adult height, whereas poorly controlled asthma itself suppresses growth. Response is reassessed at four to eight weeks with a view to stepping down after several months of good control.
key_points: Symptoms or reliever use on more than two days a week indicates poor control in a child
Night waking or exercise limitation each independently indicate the need for a preventer
Low dose inhaled corticosteroid is first line preventer treatment from age six
Long acting beta2 agonists are not appropriate as initial preventer therapy in this age group
Confirm technique, adherence and trigger exposure before every step up
explanation.pearls: Reassess a child four to eight weeks after starting a preventer and consider stepping down once control has been maintained for at least three months, because the commonest cause of an apparently unresponsive preventer at that review is a spacer that is never actually used at school.

subtopic_detail: Amenorrhoea and milk discharge in the second year of antipsychotic treatment with a prolactin level in the range that overlaps drug effect and tumour
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 27 year old woman in a community clinic. She has taken risperidone 3 mg daily for fourteen months after a single episode of psychosis and has had no symptoms for a year, and she is studying and working part time.

She tells you her periods stopped about eight months ago and that for the past three months she has noticed a milky discharge from both nipples when she showers. She has not been sexually active in that time and a urine pregnancy test today is negative. She has no headaches and no change in her vision, and confrontation visual field testing is normal. Her serum prolactin measured on two separate mornings is 1780 and 1850 mIU/L, and her thyroid stimulating hormone, follicle stimulating hormone, luteinising hormone, urea electrolytes and creatinine and liver function tests are all within normal limits. She is worried about her bones and about whether she will be able to conceive later.

data_table.Examination: Bilateral expressible milky nipple discharge, normal visual fields to confrontation, no goitre, body mass index 23 kg/m2
data_table.Investigations: Serum prolactin 1780 and 1850 mIU/L on separate mornings (less than 500), thyroid stimulating hormone 1.8 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), follicle stimulating hormone and luteinising hormone within normal limits, urea electrolytes creatinine and liver function tests within normal limits, urine pregnancy test negative
data_table.Medications: Risperidone 3 mg orally daily for fourteen months, no other prescribed or over the counter medication

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Add cabergoline 0.5 mg weekly and continue the risperidone at the current dose
options.rationale: A dopamine agonist opposes the very receptor blockade that is treating her illness and carries a real risk of precipitating psychotic relapse, so it is reserved for cases where the antipsychotic genuinely cannot be changed. Removing the cause is both safer and more effective than adding a second drug to counteract it (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Order an MRI of the pituitary before making any change to her current treatment
options.rationale: Imaging is indicated when prolactin exceeds roughly 4000 mIU/L, when there are headaches or visual field defects, or when the level fails to fall after the causative drug is changed, none of which applies to a level under 2000 mIU/L with normal fields on a known prolactin raising drug. Imaging first also delays the intervention that would both diagnose and treat (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Hyperprolactinaemia).

options.text: Switch her to aripiprazole and repeat the prolactin level after the change settles
options.rationale: Risperidone raises prolactin more than any other second generation agent because it blocks tuberoinfundibular dopamine receptors while barely crossing back out of that circulation, and aripiprazole is a partial agonist that lowers prolactin, often to normal within four to eight weeks. Repeating the level after the switch is what distinguishes drug effect from a coincidental adenoma, so the change is both treatment and diagnostic test (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Add a combined oral contraceptive pill to restore her monthly menstrual periods
options.rationale: Replacing oestrogen protects bone density and gives withdrawal bleeds but leaves the prolactin elevated, the galactorrhoea untreated and any underlying lesion unexamined. It is a reasonable adjunct only once the cause has been established and the antipsychotic cannot be altered (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Hyperprolactinaemia).

options.text: Stop all antipsychotic treatment and monitor her prolactin level once each month
options.rationale: Ceasing treatment entirely at fourteen months after a first episode carries a relapse risk of the order of 60 to 80 per cent within two years, which is a far greater harm than the endocrine side effect being treated. Switching agents achieves the same fall in prolactin while maintaining cover (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia).
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia

explanation.summary: Antipsychotic induced hyperprolactinaemia is common, under asked about and clinically consequential, producing amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea, sexual dysfunction, infertility and accelerated bone loss through hypogonadism. Risperidone, paliperidone, amisulpride and the typical antipsychotics are the strongest offenders, while aripiprazole, quetiapine and clozapine are prolactin sparing. The level itself is the main discriminator: drug induced elevation usually sits below about 2000 to 3000 mIU/L, macroprolactinomas typically produce levels above 5000 mIU/L, and any level with headache, visual field loss or failure to normalise after a drug change warrants pituitary imaging. Macroprolactin should also be considered when an asymptomatic patient has an unexplained elevation, since it is a biologically inactive complex that inflates the assay. Untreated hypogonadism in a young woman over years is the reason this cannot simply be watched.
key_points: Risperidone and paliperidone are the strongest prolactin raising second generation agents
Drug induced levels usually sit below about 2000 to 3000 mIU/L
Imaging is indicated above roughly 4000 mIU/L or with headache or visual field loss
Switching to aripiprazole both treats the problem and tests the hypothesis
Chronic hypogonadism causes bone loss, so watchful waiting is not benign
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically about periods, nipple discharge and sexual function at every antipsychotic review, since a prolactin is not on the routine metabolic monitoring panel and most patients on risperidone will not volunteer these symptoms unless asked directly.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia
